subject: English
topic: Tenses — past, present, future forms and usage

questions.stem: She _____ to the gym every morning. Choose correct tense.

options.option_text: goes
is going
has gone
went

questions.explanation: Habitual action (every morning) = simple present. 'Goes' is correct. Answer: A. Trap: B (present continuous, not habitual), C (present perfect), D (past).

questions.stem: By the time you arrive, I _____ dinner. Which tense?

options.option_text: will finish (alternative interpretation)
will have finished
finish (alternative interpretation)
am finishing (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: Before a future time (by the time you arrive), action must be complete. Future perfect: 'will have finished'. Answer: B. Trap: A (simple future, not complete), C (present), D (continuous).

questions.stem: I _____ lived here for 5 years. Correct form?

options.option_text: am (alternative interpretation)
have
am having
has (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: Duration from past to present: present perfect 'have lived'. I (first person singular) = have. Answer: B. Trap: A (am, wrong auxiliary), C (continuous), D (has, third person).

questions.stem: He _____ studying when his friend called. What tense?

options.option_text: was studying
studied (alternative interpretation)
has been studying
is studying

questions.explanation: Action in progress when interrupted: past continuous 'was studying'. Answer: A. Trap: B (simple past, not showing continuation), C (present perfect), D (present).

questions.stem: They _____ the project before the deadline. Choose tense.

options.option_text: completed (alternative interpretation)
have completed
had completed
were completing

questions.explanation: One past action before another past event: past perfect 'had completed'. Implies project completion before deadline (both in past). Answer: C. Trap: A (simple past, doesn't show precedence), B (present perfect), D (continuous).

questions.stem: By next year, I _____ this company for 10 years. Tense?

options.option_text: will work (alternative interpretation)
will have worked (alternative interpretation)
will be working (alternative interpretation)
will have been working

questions.explanation: Duration (10 years) by a future time: future perfect continuous 'will have been working'. Emphasizes duration and completion. Answer: D. Trap: B (perfect but not continuous), A (simple), C (continuous but not perfect).

questions.stem: If it _____ tomorrow, we will cancel the event. Condition?

options.option_text: rains
will rain
is raining
rained

questions.explanation: First conditional (possible future): if + simple present, will + base verb. 'If it rains' (not 'will rain'). Answer: A. Trap: B (wrong tense in if-clause), C (present continuous), D (past).

questions.stem: Choose the grammatically correct sentence regarding stative verbs:

options.option_text: The sugar was tasting sweet after the cook added it
The sugar tasted sweet after the cook added it
The sugar had been tasting sweet after the cook added it
The sugar was being tasted sweet after the cook added it

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'taste' is a stative verb (describes a sensory state, not an action) and must not be used in progressive or continuous forms. Option A ('was tasting') and C ('had been tasting') incorrectly apply progressive aspect to a stative verb. Option D is passive-progressive, doubly wrong for a stative verb. Stative verbs — know, believe, seem, taste, own — use simple tenses.

questions.stem: In reported speech, 'He told me, I am preparing for the exam' becomes which of the following?

options.option_text: He told me he is preparing for the exam
He told me he was preparing for the exam
He told me he had been preparing for the exam
He told me he prepared for the exam

questions.explanation: B is correct: when the reporting verb is past tense ('told'), the embedded verb must backshift one step — present continuous 'am preparing' becomes past continuous 'was preparing'. Option A fails to backshift at all, a common error. Option C over-backshifts to past perfect continuous, skipping a step. Option D uses simple past and loses the ongoing-action nuance of the original.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically INCORRECT in its use of the past habitual form?

options.option_text: My grandfather would walk five miles to school every day
She would be an excellent dancer in her youth
We used to spend summers at our grandmother's village
He used to smoke heavily before his doctor's warning

questions.explanation: B is incorrect: 'would' can only express repeated past actions, NOT past states or conditions. 'She would be a dancer' is wrong — 'She used to be a dancer' is required. Option A is valid because 'walk' is a habitual past action. Options C and D correctly use 'used to', which works for both past habits and discontinued states. This would/used-to distinction is a frequent SSC and IBPS exam trap.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that correctly uses the future perfect continuous tense:

options.option_text: By evening, he will finish cooking the entire meal
By evening, he will have been cooking for six hours
By evening, he will be cooking the meal since noon
By evening, he would have cooked the entire meal already

questions.explanation: B is correct: future perfect continuous = will + have + been + V-ing, expressing an action that will be ongoing up to a future reference point. Option A ('will finish') uses simple future, with no continuous aspect. Option C mixes future continuous with 'since', which is grammatically inconsistent — 'since' requires a perfect form. Option D uses conditional 'would have cooked', not future perfect continuous.

questions.stem: The detective _____ the case for two months when the key witness finally came forward. Choose the correct verb form.

options.option_text: was investigating — past continuous, ongoing at one point
investigated — simple past, no prior duration implied
had been investigating — past perfect continuous here
has been investigating — present perfect continuous used

questions.explanation: C is correct: past perfect continuous (had been + V-ing) expresses a continuous action that was ongoing over a duration before another completed past event ('came forward'). Option A ('was investigating') describes an action in progress at a moment but misses the prior-duration-before-past-event relationship. Option B (simple past) carries no durational nuance. Option D wrongly uses present perfect, implying the investigation is still continuing now.

questions.stem: The officer confirmed that the fort _____ successive invasions over four centuries. Which tense is required given the past reporting verb?

options.option_text: had withstood — past perfect, correctly backshifted form
has withstood — present perfect, not backshifted here
withstood — simple past, loses the completion nuance
was withstanding — past continuous, wrong aspect used

questions.explanation: A is correct: the reporting verb 'confirmed' is past tense, so the embedded clause must backshift — present perfect 'has withstood' → past perfect 'had withstood' (sequence-of-tenses rule). Option B ('has withstood') breaks this rule and is the most tempting distractor. Option C ('withstood') uses simple past and loses the perfective aspect — completion before a reference point. Option D ('was withstanding') wrongly applies continuous aspect to the achievement verb 'withstand'.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly expresses regret about a past action using the 'wish' construction?

options.option_text: I wish I studied harder for the entrance exam last year
I wish I had studied harder for the entrance exam last year
I wish I would have studied harder for the entrance exam
I wish I was studying harder during the entrance exam

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'wish' + past perfect expresses regret about a past situation that can no longer be changed. Option A uses simple past after 'wish', which is reserved for present unreal situations (e.g., 'I wish I knew the answer'). Option C ('would have') after 'wish' is a widespread non-standard error — 'would' is never used in the wish-clause when referring to past regret; this construction is specifically tested in SSC CGL. Option D ('was studying') uses past progressive, incompatible with the completed-event regret structure.
